passage: I'm Darshan and I share a flat with Jagdish. For three weeks I watched Jagdish wait for the right conditions to write the thesis chapter. First it was the desk: too cluttered, so Jagdish tidied it and bought a new lamp. Then it was time: “I need a whole free day.” The free day came on Sunday, and Jagdish said the mood wasn't right. Then it was a new pen. The desk stayed clear and the document stayed empty. I don't know what was going on in Jagdish's mind, maybe worry about the chapter being not good enough. When I asked, the answer was, “Once everything is set, it will flow.” Everything never seemed to be set.

qa.q: What did Jagdish buy while waiting for the right conditions?
qa.a: Jagdish bought a new lamp and a new pen.

qa.q: What might Jagdish be feeling behind “once everything is set, it will flow”?
qa.a: Jagdish may be anxious or afraid the chapter won't be good enough, though Darshan cannot be sure; the waiting looks like a polite name for postponing.

qa.q: What could Jagdish try to break the pattern?
qa.a: Sit down at the ordinary messy desk for a set half hour and write a rough page, without waiting for the day, the mood or a new pen.

qa.q: How does Darshan see Jagdish's waiting?
qa.a: Darshan is watchful and a little worried, noticing the tidy desk and empty document and guessing at worry rather than laziness.

grounding: A young adult waits for a clear desk, a free day and the right mood before starting a thesis chapter.

passage:
Day 1: Chinmay cleared the desk, put a fresh notebook beside the laptop and said to Uma in the library, “I'll begin the chapter tomorrow, when I've got the whole morning.”

Day 9: The whole morning had not appeared. Chinmay now said, “Saturday, when the hostel is empty and quiet.” Saturday, a pigeon cooed outside, and someone played music down the corridor, and the quiet wasn't right.

Day 20: Uma found Chinmay on a crowded bus with a phone open on a note app, typing in half-sentences. “Two hundred words,” Chinmay said, pleased, not looking up. “On a bus.”

qa.q: Where did Chinmay tell Uma about beginning the chapter?
qa.a: Chinmay told Uma in the library.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay keep moving the start date?
qa.a: Chinmay felt uneasy about the big chapter and relieved each time the start moved, so waiting for perfect conditions became a way of postponing it.

qa.q: What happened on Day 20 that had not happened before?
qa.a: Chinmay wrote two hundred words on a crowded bus, in half-sentences on a phone, without a clear desk, a whole morning or quiet.

qa.q: How might Uma feel finding Chinmay typing on the bus?
qa.a: Uma is probably surprised and glad, having seen the waiting for weeks and now seeing real words appear.

grounding: A young adult waits for a clear desk, a full day and quiet before a thesis chapter, and begins only when conditions are imperfect.

passage:
Sunday, 11 pm.
Thesis chapter 2 still not started. Today's reasons: the desk was covered in laundry, and by the time I cleared it, it was 3 pm, which is "not a full day". Yesterday the reason was a headache. Last week, Gurpreet was visiting and I needed "the right mood".
I keep waiting for a morning where my desk is clean, my head is clear and I have eight free hours. It has never happened. Not once in two months.
Gurpreet said something before leaving: "You're not waiting for conditions. You're waiting to not be scared." That stung.
Tomorrow: 9 am, messy desk, one paragraph. Whatever mood I'm in.
Nikita

qa.q: What was covering Nikita's desk on Sunday?
qa.a: The desk was covered in laundry.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel about Gurpreet's comment?
qa.a: It stung; Nikita felt hurt but also recognised the truth that the waiting was about fear.

qa.q: What plan does Nikita make, and why could it work?
qa.a: Starting at 9 am with a messy desk and just one paragraph drops the demand for perfect conditions, which never arrive.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have seen the visit and the unstarted chapter?
qa.a: Gurpreet seems to have noticed that the reasons kept changing and guessed that fear, not conditions, was the real block.

grounding: A diary shows a young adult waiting for a clear desk, a full day and the right mood before starting a thesis chapter.

passage:
Sunaina: did you start the dissertation chapter?
Maria: not yet. waiting for the weekend
Sunaina: you said that last weekend
Maria: last weekend my room was a mess. you can't write in chaos
Sunaina: and the weekend before?
Maria: I had a cold. need a clear head for methodology
Sunaina: Maria. it's been 5 weekends
Maria: I know 😔 I just want a proper full day with nothing else
Sunaina: when did you last have one of those
Maria: ...march?
Sunaina: so the perfect day is basically a myth
Maria: rude but ok
Sunaina: library tomorrow 2-4. messy notes allowed. I'll sit with you
Maria: 2 hours isn't enough to do anything
Sunaina: it's enough to start
Maria: fine. 2 pm

qa.q: How many weekends had passed without Maria starting?
qa.a: It had been 5 weekends.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when Sunaina pointed out the five weekends?
qa.a: Maria felt sad and a bit embarrassed, still wishing for a proper full day with nothing else.

qa.q: What did Sunaina offer, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: Two hours in the library with messy notes allowed, which gives Maria a start in imperfect conditions instead of waiting for the ideal day.

qa.q: How does Sunaina see Maria's reasons?
qa.a: Sunaina sees them as ways of postponing, since the perfect day has not come since March, and gently calls it out.

grounding: A chat shows a student repeatedly waiting for a clear room, a clear head and a full day before starting a dissertation chapter.

passage: Damini, twenty-two, was writing a dissertation on water use for her college in Satara while living at home in the village. The chapter on farmers' interviews was due in a month. She told herself she needed the right setup: the electricity steady, the courtyard quiet, the whole day free. Every morning something broke the picture: the buffalo needed feeding, a neighbour came by, the power went off. Her friend Ankita, a schoolteacher, visited one afternoon and found her sorting pens. "Write in the noise," Ankita said. "I correct forty notebooks with children shouting." Damini laughed, then sat on the step with her notebook. She wrote a page by lamplight that evening.

qa.q: What was Damini's dissertation about?
qa.a: It was a dissertation on water use.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when Ankita found her sorting pens?
qa.a: She felt stuck and a bit defensive, still waiting for a quiet, full day that never came.

qa.q: Which choice finally helped Damini start?
qa.a: Sitting on the step and writing despite the noise and the lamp, instead of waiting for steady electricity and a free day.

qa.q: How does Ankita see the wait for perfect conditions?
qa.a: Ankita, who corrects notebooks amid children's shouting, sees it as unnecessary and encourages Damini to write anyway.

grounding: Shows a young adult waiting for ideal conditions to start a dissertation chapter, until she writes despite the noise.

passage: Paulo had a theory about the methods chapter of his thesis: it needed a clean run. Not an hour squeezed between café shifts in Johannesburg, but a whole Saturday, coffee made, phone in a drawer, the washing done so it wouldn't nag him. The first Saturday, Lindiwe's cousins came to visit. The second, he had a cold and said his head wasn't right for it. On the third, the sun was out and staying indoors felt like a waste. "You're waiting for the chapter to roll out a welcome mat," Lindiwe said, stirring a pot on the stove. On Tuesday his supervisor emailed: meeting Friday, bring a draft. Paulo wrote four messy pages at the kitchen table on Wednesday night, crumbs everywhere. They were not good, but they existed.

qa.q: What did Paulo want before starting the methods chapter?
qa.a: A whole Saturday, with coffee made, the phone in a drawer and the washing done.

qa.q: What might Paulo have felt when the supervisor's email arrived?
qa.a: Probably alarmed and a little ashamed, because three Saturdays had passed and he had nothing to bring on Friday.

qa.q: What could Paulo try instead of waiting for a perfect Saturday?
qa.a: He could write for the hour between café shifts, even messily, since the Wednesday pages showed that imperfect time still produces a draft.

qa.q: How does Lindiwe see Paulo's plan?
qa.a: Lindiwe sees the perfect Saturday as an excuse that keeps moving and teases about a welcome mat, amused but also a bit frustrated watching the weeks slip.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who keeps waiting for ideal conditions to start a thesis chapter and finds those conditions never arrive.
